strengths: As an Algorithms/General submission, the paper presents a coherent visual-inertial Gaussian-splatting SLAM system that combines dense DROID-style correspondence optimization, IMU preintegration, staged initialization, loop closure, and efficient map correction.
The practical problem is important: IMU measurements directly address motion blur, low texture, frame drops, and rapid motion that commonly undermine monocular Gaussian-splatting SLAM.

Evaluation is broad, covering 32 sequences across four datasets with indoor/outdoor, handheld, drone, and robot settings. Results are generally strong for both trajectory accuracy and novel-view rendering.

The strided-frame experiments are particularly useful. Reporting trajectory recall alongside ATE avoids making partially tracked trajectories appear successful, and shows a substantial robustness benefit from inertial fusion.
The supplementary material provides per-sequence results, runtime measurements, dataset statistics, major hyperparameters, and results before and after optional global refinement.
The loop-closure Gaussian update is simple and computationally attractive, and its mapping ablation supports its practical value. The paper is generally clear and visually well organized.
weaknesses: The central novelty is incremental. Most ingredients—DROID-style dense BA, standard IMU preintegration and bias estimation, Sim(3) pose-graph optimization, and keyframe-anchored Gaussian transformations—are established techniques. The paper does not experimentally isolate whether its particular tight coupling is superior to a reasonably implemented loose or alternating fusion design.

Comparison to the closest visual-inertial Gaussian-SLAM systems is inadequate. VINGS-Mono and GI-SLAM are discussed but not evaluated, while MM3DGS-SLAM is compared only through incomplete published UTMM numbers. Consequently, the strongest empirical evidence is largely against RGB-only Gaussian systems or classical sparse VIO, and does not fully establish the claimed advantage over prior visual-inertial Gaussian approaches.

The ablations do not cover several claimed contributions: staged IMU initialization, per-keyframe/time-varying biases, online Jacobian corrections, inertial uncertainty fallback, or tight versus decoupled optimization. The reported tracking ablation is confined to artificially strided EuRoC, and the mapping ablation to FAST-LIVO2.

The optimization is underspecified. No relative weighting or robustification between visual and inertial objectives is given, nor are marginalization/window management and numerical solution details. Equation (2) also appears dimensionally or notationally inconsistent: a joint rotation/position/velocity/bias residual is weighted by a preintegration covariance that is not defined to include bias random-walk terms, and the velocity bias correction is written using only the gyroscope bias.

The “real-time” claim is not convincingly supported. On an RTX 5090, full tracking plus Gaussian mapping averages only 7.09 FPS on 30-FPS RPNG data, while tracking alone averages 16.4 FPS. The paper does not explain queueing, latency, dropped frames, or whether online processing can keep pace with the sensor stream.

Evaluation protocol details limit confidence: the trajectory alignment degrees of freedom are unspecified, no repeated-run statistics are reported for learned or initialization-sensitive systems, baseline configuration/restart policies are not sufficiently standardized, and FAST-LIVO2 provides only pseudo-ground truth from a LiDAR-visual-inertial estimator.

Reproducibility remains limited: the project-page field is blank, code availability is not stated, calibration and temporal synchronization procedures are omitted, and some IMU processing is acknowledged to remain in NumPy. These omissions matter for a tightly coupled sensor-fusion system.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant gap: combining monocular visual-inertial estimation with dense, photorealistic 3D Gaussian mapping. The integration of DROID-SLAM-style dense correspondence optimization, IMU preintegration, staged initialization, loop closure, and Gaussian-map correction forms a coherent end-to-end system.

The evaluation is broad, covering EuRoC, RPNG, UTMM, and FAST-LIVO2, with both indoor and outdoor sequences. VIGS-SLAM obtains strong tracking results, including 2.79 cm average ATE on EuRoC and substantial improvements on the more difficult UTMM sequences.

The frame-striding experiments are useful because they directly probe the claimed benefit of inertial sensing when visual observations become sparse. The per-sequence recall results also expose partial tracking failures that ATE alone could obscure.

The paper evaluates both tracking and rendering, includes component ablations, reports results before optional offline refinement, and provides reasonably clear system diagrams and supplementary per-sequence tables.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited for an Algorithms/General contribution. Most components—DROID-SLAM visual residuals, conventional IMU preintegration and staged initialization, pose-graph loop closure, and keyframe-anchored Gaussian transformations—are adaptations or combinations of established techniques. The paper does not isolate a sufficiently distinctive technical insight beyond their integration.

Experimental comparison against the closest contemporary visual-inertial Gaussian SLAM systems is inadequate. VINGS-Mono and GI-SLAM are discussed but never evaluated, while MM3DGS-SLAM is compared only through incomplete reported UTMM results. Consequently, the experiments establish an advantage over visual-only and classical VIO baselines more convincingly than over the closest prior art.

The claimed real-time operation is not demonstrated. On an RTX 5090, the complete tracking-and-mapping system averages only 7.09 FPS on the 30-FPS RPNG data, and tracking alone averages 16.40 FPS. This is substantially slower than the input rate, yet the abstract and conclusion repeatedly characterize the system as real-time.

Important technical details are underspecified or potentially inconsistent. The inertial velocity residual shows a bias correction involving only the gyroscope bias although velocity preintegration normally depends on accelerometer bias; the covariance treatment of the concatenated motion and bias residuals is not explained. Likewise, the Sim(3) loop-closure update optimizes poses and disparities, but the paper does not explain how velocities, biases, gravity, and subsequent inertial residuals remain consistent after scale corrections.

The robustness claims are overstated. Although the method is markedly better at moderate subsampling, its EuRoC Recall@10cm falls to 29.40% at stride 20 and 6.87% at stride 40; the corresponding RPNG values are 74.37% and 24.26%. Thus it does not remain broadly stable under the most extreme settings shown.

The evaluation lacks repeated-run statistics or uncertainty, despite learned SLAM pipelines and initialization being potentially variable. Some EuRoC baseline values are copied from earlier papers while others are reproduced, which weakens protocol comparability. FAST-LIVO2 and the self-captured sequence additionally use LiDAR-based pseudo-ground truth rather than independent ground truth.

The rendering evaluation is only against visual Gaussian-SLAM baselines and uses non-keyframe images from the same trajectories, which are nearby rather than genuinely novel viewpoints. Keyframe-selection differences, evaluation-frame construction, and failed sequences can materially affect these averages; Table 3 even omits an average for HI-SLAM2 on RPNG instead of specifying a consistent failure-aware aggregation.

The ablations do not adequately substantiate the main design decisions. Tracking ablations are restricted to EuRoC at one artificial stride, mapping ablation examines only the Gaussian loop update on FAST-LIVO2, and there is no comparison of tight joint optimization against a decoupled factor-graph alternative, fixed versus time-varying bias, staged versus simpler initialization, or PGBA design choices.

Reproducibility is presently weak: the project-page field is blank, no code or release commitment is provided, and essential settings such as loss weights, local-window size, optimization iterations, solver details, sensor synchronization/calibration handling, and several failure criteria are missing. Overall, the promising empirical system is not yet supported by sufficiently novel methodology, closest-baseline evidence, or real-time validation for acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a practically important visual-inertial 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM system. Its tight joint optimization of poses, disparities, velocities, and time-varying IMU biases, together with staged initialization and loop-consistent Gaussian updates, forms a coherent technical contribution beyond simply attaching IMU pose estimates to a visual pipeline.

The empirical evaluation is broad and unusually challenging: 32 sequences across EuRoC, RPNG, UTMM, and FAST-LIVO2 cover indoor and outdoor settings, different platforms, low texture, blur, illumination changes, and large-scale motion.

Tracking performance is strong. The method obtains the best reported average online ATE on all four datasets, including 2.79 cm on EuRoC, 1.68 cm on RPNG, 3.24 cm on UTMM, and 6.08 cm on FAST-LIVO2, while avoiding the initialization failures seen in several baselines.

The strided-frame experiments provide convincing evidence for the central claim that IMU fusion improves robustness when visual observations degrade. At stride 10, VIGS-SLAM retains 98.99% Recall@10cm on EuRoC and 100% on RPNG, substantially exceeding the compared visual and visual-inertial systems.

The system addresses both localization and photorealistic mapping. It consistently improves PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over Splat-SLAM and HI-SLAM2 before offline color refinement, and the qualitative results show visibly sharper textures and fewer artifacts.

Ablations support the usefulness of IMU fusion, loop closure, IMU-based keyframe initialization, and the Gaussian-map correction after loop closure. Reporting both pre- and post-global-refinement results also makes the online/offline distinction relatively transparent.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, provides equations for the principal residuals and map update, discloses common hyperparameters and hardware, and explicitly acknowledges the high-end-GPU and camera-model limitations.
weaknesses: The novelty is primarily a careful systems integration of DROID-SLAM-style dense visual optimization, standard IMU preintegration, pose-graph loop closure, and Gaussian mapping. The paper should more precisely distinguish its algorithmic novelty from the closest visual-inertial Gaussian systems, especially VINGS-Mono, GI-SLAM, MM3DGS-SLAM, and VIGS-Fusion.

The most relevant recent systems are discussed but not evaluated quantitatively, leaving uncertainty about whether the gains arise from tight coupling and time-varying bias estimation specifically or simply from adding IMU information to a strong DROID/HI-SLAM2 foundation. An ablation against a loosely coupled or fixed-bias variant would materially strengthen the contribution.

The “real-time” characterization is somewhat overstated. On an RTX 5090, the complete tracking-plus-mapping system averages only 7.09 FPS on 30-FPS RPNG data and drops to 4.36 FPS on one sequence. The paper attributes some cost to an unoptimized NumPy implementation, but projected CUDA performance is not evidence of current real-time operation.

Several reproducibility details remain underspecified, including objective weights for visual versus inertial terms, solver and marginalization settings, synchronization and calibration handling, failure/restart criteria, and memory or map-growth behavior. The project-page link is also blank in the submitted manuscript, and no code-release commitment is stated.

The ablation evidence is narrower than the headline list of contributions: tracking ablations are reported only on stride-10 EuRoC, and there is no direct isolation of staged initialization, per-keyframe bias modeling, Jacobian bias correction, or joint optimization versus alternating optimization.

Evaluation methodology would benefit from repeated trials and dispersion statistics, particularly because learned SLAM pipelines and initialization can be stochastic. Some baseline numbers are copied from earlier papers while others are reproduced, which may introduce configuration and hardware inconsistencies.

The scalability of loop detection and mapping is unclear. Comparing every new keyframe with earlier keyframes using optical flow and continually adding Gaussians may become expensive on long trajectories, yet runtime is measured only on relatively short tabletop sequences and neither memory consumption nor long-run map size is reported.

FAST-LIVO2 and the self-captured extreme sequence use FAST-LIVO2 trajectories as pseudo-ground truth, so those experiments are not fully independent validations. The self-captured evidence is also limited to one sequence.

There appears to be a notation issue in the inertial formulation: the velocity preintegration correction is written only in terms of gyroscope bias even though preintegrated velocity normally depends on accelerometer bias as well. This may be a presentation error, but the equations should be checked and corrected.
